title: It's Not the Explanations
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane pushes back against Zach Groshell's book Just Tell Them, arguing that its title and framing overstate the centrality of explanations to effective explicit teaching. Examining three exemplars of explicit instruction - Direct Instruction scripts, Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, and the JUMP Math curriculum - Kane shows that explanation is a minor, largely obvious component in each; the real engine is the structured system of questions, worked examples, guided practice, and checks for understanding that gets students actively doing the thinking. He argues that teachers already know explanations exist and use them, so framing explicit teaching as fundamentally about 'telling' does a disservice to the far less obvious and far more powerful moves - breaking content into small steps, connecting prior knowledge, guiding and checking practice - that actually produce learning. Kane's own practice reflects this: he has shifted over a decade toward explaining less and having students do more math. The piece closes with a caution against reducing any complex teaching approach to one memorable but misleading catchphrase.
points: Kane's central claim: across Direct Instruction, Rosenshine's Principles, and JUMP Math, explanation is a small and largely obvious component of explicit teaching, not its center - the center is the questions and tasks students are given.
In Rosenshine's ten principles, the only one where explanation is clearly present is 'Provide models' - the rest concern practice, feedback, scaffolding, and review, not teacher talk.
JUMP Math explicitly downplays explanations, instead breaking concepts into small incremental steps with practice after each, letting students discover patterns through guided problem-solving.

Kane's practical takeaway from his own teaching: reducing explanation time in favor of more structured student practice ('I explain less; students do math more') has been one of the most significant shifts in his teaching over the last decade.

His broader warning: catchy framings like 'just tell them' risk convincing teachers that explicit instruction is mostly about talking, when the harder, less obvious work - sequencing, practice design, and checks for understanding - is what actually drives learning.
quotes: But the book falls into a trap that I find unhelpful. Groshell advocates for a type of teaching that is often called explicit teaching or direct instruction or some other permutation of those words.

You can feel however you like about Direct Instruction. There's a lot to have opinions about -- the scripting, the procedural focus, the whole-group choral response, the fast-paced whole-group instruction. But explanations are not the central component of this style of teaching.

Rosenshine's principles are often held up as a model for explicit teaching. But here's the thing. Explanation doesn't play a very large role. The only principle where explanation is clearly present is "Provide models.
To me, the center of teaching is all the questions and tasks we give students. We want students to do stuff -- in my case, to solve math problems -- in order to learn.
I explain less; students do math more. Again, I'm not saying I don't explain things. I do. But explanations are not the center of effective teaching.

Teaching well involves doings lots of things well, and fitting all those things into a coherent system. It will always be tempting to reduce teaching down to that one little thing. But that's not how it works.
